briefOverview: Paul and Barnabas preach across Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe, facing both belief and fierce opposition. A healing in Lystra leads to attempted pagan worship, persecution, and then strengthening of new churches with appointed elders.
summary: In Iconium many Jews and Greeks believe, but opposition rises, forcing Paul and Barnabas to flee after a plot to stone them. In Lystra Paul heals a man lame from birth, prompting locals to hail them as gods (Jupiter and Mercurius), which the apostles reject, urging the crowd to turn from idols to the living Creator whose providence is seen in rain and harvests. Despite their protest, visiting opponents stir up the crowd, and Paul is stoned and left for dead, but he rises and departs to Derbe. After preaching in Derbe, they retrace their steps, encouraging disciples to continue in the faith and teaching that entry into God’s kingdom comes through many tribulations. They appoint elders in each church with prayer and fasting, entrusting them to the Lord, then travel back to Antioch in Syria. There they report how God opened a door of faith to the Gentiles and remain there for a considerable time.
externalContext: This chapter sits in Paul and Barnabas’s first missionary journey (Acts 13–14), launched from Antioch in Syria, a major center of early Gentile Christianity. Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe were cities in the Roman province of Galatia or adjacent regions (Lycaonia) in south-central Anatolia, where Greek, Latin, and local languages (e.g., Lycaonian) were spoken. Identification of the apostles with Jupiter (Zeus) and Mercurius (Hermes) reflects common Greco-Roman cults; Hermes was often seen as the spokesman of the gods. Stoning was a traditional Jewish form of execution, but in the Roman world such violence could emerge from mob action rather than formal legal process. Early Christian communities adapted familiar Jewish leadership structures, appointing elders (presbyteroi) to oversee local congregations.
externalReferences: Paul’s healing of a man lame from birth mirrors Peter’s earlier healing at the temple gate (Acts 3:2–8), highlighting continuity in apostolic signs. Paul’s appeal to the Creator who gives rain and fruitful seasons resonates with natural revelation themes (Romans 1:19–20) and anticipates the Areopagus speech’s emphasis on God as Creator and sustainer (Acts 17:24–27). The report that God opened “a door of faith” to the Gentiles echoes the church’s earlier recognition after Cornelius that God grants life to Gentiles as well (Acts 11:18). The appointment of elders in every church parallels later instructions about establishing local leadership (Titus 1:5).
practicalQuestions: How can I speak about God in ways that connect with my audience’s background without compromising the message?
When is it wise to flee danger versus remain and face opposition for the sake of the mission?
How can I avoid receiving inappropriate credit or “celebrity” and redirect honor to God?
What habits help me persevere in faith when opposition or suffering arises?
How can local churches develop trustworthy leaders and entrust them to God through prayer and fasting?
uncertainAreas: The phrase “priest of Jupiter… before their city” may refer to a temple location near the gates, but the exact setting is unclear. The crowd’s assumption that Paul was dead after stoning is narrated from their perspective; whether he briefly lost consciousness or was miraculously preserved is unstated. The method implied by “ordained them elders” (cheirotonesantes) is debated—whether by apostolic appointment or congregational recognition. Durations of the “long time” spent in Iconium and at Antioch are not specified.
